current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.
current_affected_interface_subjects.current_strategy: The ordinary vector FTC and integral triangle inequality give $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\le v_*|s_2-s_1|$. For fixed $x$ put $g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$. It is continuous and for $s_2>s_1$ satisfies $g_x(s_2)-g_x(s_1)\ge(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)>0$. Consequently $g_x(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$; IVT and strict monotonicity give a unique solution of $g_x(s)=t$. Since $g_x(s)\ge s$, $s\le t$, and equality is equivalent to $x=z(t)$. On $D$ the root has $r>0$. Continuity of $z$ makes $D$ open. Near any root on $D$, $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ has precisely the regularity of $z$, because the Euclidean norm is smooth away from zero. Its $s$ derivative is $-\kappa$, bounded away from zero. Apply the parametrized implicit-function theorem with its actual $C^1$ hypothesis first, or with $C^k$ when $z$ is $C^k$; global uniqueness glues these local maps. Differentiating $F=0$ gives the two stated formulas. Repeat for every finite $k$ in the smooth case. Do not infer $C^3$ from $C^1$, and do not exclude an observation point merely because the trajectory visits it at a different time. The exact non-improvement witness is a small uniformly subluminal $z(s)=(\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2},0,0)$ with smooth compact cutoff $\chi=1$ near zero. At a distant positive axial point $L>\sup|z|$, the retardation map is $g(s)=s+(L-\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2})/c$, $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at zero. A $C^2$ inverse near $t=L/c$, whose derivative is nonzero, would make $g$ $C^2$ by the inverse-function theorem, a contradiction.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$ and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (entrywise integrability), and let $$\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0)$$ be the matrix response function. Here locally absolutely continuous means that each real entry restricted to every compact interval $[a,b]\subseteq[0,\infty)$ satisfies the finite disjoint-interval condition of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]: for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\sum_\ell(v_\ell-u_\ell)<\delta$ implies $\sum_\ell|K_{jk}(v_\ell)-K_{jk}(u_\ell)|<\epsilon$ for every finite family with disjoint interiors. $K\prime$ denotes the almost-everywhere derivative, with any measurable zero extension on its null exceptional set. Then the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-domain]]), continuous and $C^1$ on its real boundary, bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and the entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas hold: for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi .$$ The sharper bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le(|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K\prime_{jk}\|_1)/|z|$ holds for every nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. Here $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$ means $\lim_{R\to\infty}\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}(\int_{\omega-R}^{\omega-\eta}+\int_{\omega+\eta}^{\omega+R})F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$; the tails converge absolutely, so the choice of centering at infinity does not change the limit. For an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define the total transfer function $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$; the formulas then apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Causality alone supplies neither growth assumptions beyond those stated nor the passivity quadratic-form condition, which is a separate model assertion.
current_affected_interface_subjects.current_strategy:
Treat each real entry $k=K_{jk}$ separately. Its locally absolutely continuous representative is the one in the statement; the published [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] applies on $[0,N]$ under the declared Countable Choice and Dependent Choice and yields $k(s)=k(0)+\int_0^s k\prime(u)du$. Since $k\prime\in L^1$, dominated convergence shows this has a finite limit $\ell=k(0)+\int_0^\infty k\prime$. If $\ell\ne0$, then $|k(s)|\ge|\ell|/2$ for all sufficiently large $s$, contradicting $k\in L^1$ by monotonicity of the integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Hence $k(s)\to0$.
The defining integral is bounded by $\|k\|_1$ on $\overline H$, and dominated convergence gives joint continuity there ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Writing $z=x+iy$, the real parameter derivatives of $k(s)e^{izs}$ are $isk(s)e^{izs}$ and $-sk(s)e^{izs}$. On any rectangle in $H$ their absolute values are bounded by $s|k(s)|$, integrable by hypothesis. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied separately in $x,y$ supplies the partials; dominated convergence makes them continuous, and $\partial_y\chi=i\partial_x\chi$ gives holomorphy by [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]]. Along the real boundary the same theorem in the real parameter and the same majorant give the continuous derivative $\chi\prime(\omega)=\int_0^\infty isk(s)e^{i\omega s}ds$.
For fixed $z\ne0$, the real and imaginary parts of $g(s):=e^{izs}$ are $C^1$ on each $[0,N]$, hence absolutely continuous by [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]]. Apply [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] separately to $(k,\operatorname{Re}g)$ and $(k,\operatorname{Im}g)$ and combine the real identities to get
$$\int_0^N k(s)e^{izs}ds=\frac{k(N)e^{izN}-k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^N k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds.$$
This is Lebesgue integration by parts for AC functions, not the ordinary everywhere-differentiable Riemann theorem. For $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, $|e^{izs}|\le1$; $k(N)\to0$ kills the endpoint term and dominated convergence applies to both integrals. Thus
$$\chi_{jk}(z)=-\frac{k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^\infty k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds,\qquad |\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\frac{|k(0)|+\|k\prime\|_1}{|z|}.$$
For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $F$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $F(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $F(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $F$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $F(z+i\delta)\to F(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $F(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi F(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[F(\xi)-F(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi F(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply the preceding step to each entry of $\chi$. Adding the stipulated real instantaneous matrix means the total transfer function is $\chi_\infty+\chi$; subtract $\chi_\infty$ before taking the principal values. All scalar claims are the $d=1$ case. Neither temporal causality nor these analytic identities impose the separate passivity quadratic-form condition.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory, and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ open containing its graph. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$, $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$, is proper: the inverse image of every compact subset of $\Omega$ is compact in $I$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_I z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. These define distributions and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, or if $I=\mathbb R$. Endpoint variant: if $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite, and both endpoint events belong to $\Omega$, the same integrals instead define distributions with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)}$. A finite-history source is source-free only when the endpoint contribution vanishes on the chosen test domain; neither mere graph containment nor test compactness alone supplies this.
current_affected_interface_subjects.current_strategy: For a fixed compact test support $K\subset\Omega$, properness makes $\gamma^{-1}(K)$ compact in $I$. It lies in one closed interior interval $[u,v]\subset I$, on which $z'$ is bounded. Both pairings are bounded by constants depending on $K$ times $\sup_K|\psi|$, proving distribution continuity on each test-support space. The pullback of a test is $C^1$ and compactly supported in $I$. By the total chain rule, pairing the divergence gives $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]dt=-q\int_I(d/dt)\psi(z(t),t)dt=0$ by interior FTC. For $I=\mathbb R$, compact ambient support bounds the time coordinate and its graph preimage is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R$; for $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, compact ambient support has time projection compact inside $I$. This proves both automatic properness claims. In the endpoint variant, finite interval length and the finite absolute improper integral of $z'$ bound the pairings on every compact test support. Apply the chain rule and FTC on $[a+\epsilon,b-\epsilon]$; the derivative pullback is absolutely integrable, and continuity at endpoints gives the limiting identity $q\psi(z(a),a)-q\psi(z(b),b)$. This proves the two endpoint deltas. In particular $I=(0,1),z=0,\Omega=\mathbb R^4$ gives $q\delta_{(0,0)}-q\delta_{(0,1)}$, refuting the old unconditional claim. The endpoint integration limit is explicitly this truncation argument, not an invented source reading. Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted. Here the two-ended improper integral means the sum of the limits of integrals on [a+epsilon,r] and [r,b−epsilon] for any fixed interior r. Monotonicity and completeness prove convergence of every nonnegative integrand bounded by a constant times 1+|z′|; signed limits then follow from the positive and negative parts. Thus the endpoint variant uses only the explicitly supplied improper convention and truncated ordinary FTC.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $\omega_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\chi$ be holomorphic on the upper half-plane and continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on its real boundary away from $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfying $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set ([[def-complex-domain]]). Let $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)(z-\omega_0)^j/j!$ be the Taylor polynomial at $\omega_0$ and $f(z)=[\chi(z)-P(z)]/(z-\omega_0)^n$, with the removable value at $\omega_0$. Assume the boundary restriction of $f$ is class $C^1$ (the local holomorphy supplies this at $\omega_0$). Then for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Re}P(\omega)+\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,$$ $$\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}P(\omega)-\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi.$$ At $\omega=\omega_0$ the formula is read as the stated Taylor value. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is also valid with $P=0$, $f=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and the factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ for all $\omega$; at $\omega_0$ use the same principal-value formula rather than a Taylor-value convention. For the separate constitutive polynomial branch assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]), let $A_0,\ldots,A_m$ be real scalar coefficients or real matrices, and let $K$ satisfy all hypotheses of [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]. On histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$, the response $\sum_{j=0}^m A_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ is causal, and its transfer function in the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z):=\sum_{j=0}^m A_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared polynomial $Q$ leaves the proved entrywise dispersion formulas for $\chi_K$; this branch does not require holomorphic continuation through a real subtraction point. The Taylor-subtracted formulas above apply to the total response when its additional local-holomorphy, growth and boundary hypotheses are satisfied; $Q$ need not equal its Taylor polynomial $P$. General passivity and storage remain separate model conditions.

Elsewhere in $H$ its denominator is nonzero. Continuity of $\chi$ on $\overline H$ and the removable continuation make $f$ continuous on $\overline H$; its real restriction is $C^1$ by hypothesis. The growth bound on $\chi$ and the degree of $P$ give $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly in $\overline H$ at infinity. For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $f$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $f(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $f$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $f(z+i\delta)\to f(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $f(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi f(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[f(\xi)-f(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi f(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply that boundary-contour argument to $f$, multiply both formulas by the real factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^n$, and add the complex polynomial $P$. At $\omega_0$ the factor vanishes and the removable Taylor identity gives the asserted Taylor value. The imaginary numerator subtracts the full complex $P$; it cannot be omitted.
For the distinct constitutive branch, multiplication by $(-i\omega)^j$ is the derivative multiplier on the stipulated monochromatic histories, so the transfer polynomial is exactly $Q$. Derivatives at a time are determined by a history agreeing on its whole past, including its endpoint, and the convolution is causal; hence their finite sum is causal on histories with the stated bounded continuous derivatives. The residual $\chi-Q=\chi_K$ satisfies [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]] entrywise. Without that lemma's AC and integrability conditions a merely integrable causal kernel still gives a bounded upper-half-plane holomorphic response, but does not automatically supply these principal values or Taylor continuation. The stated additional analytic assumptions, not causality alone, govern the Taylor branch.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the smooth Riemann/Lebesgue comparison route below; in clause (c), also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) inherited from the AC supplier. Let $d\ge1$. All kernels below are real $d\times d$ matrix kernels and all histories are $\mathbb R^d$-valued; conditions on matrices are read entrywise, and $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ means entrywise Lebesgue integrability on $(0,\infty)$.

(a) (Causal convolution.) Let $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and continuous. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the integral $P(t):=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely, $$|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d\Bigl(\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|E_k(s)|\Bigr)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d),$$ the response $P$ is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$, then their responses coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

(b) (Compact branch.) If $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (smooth, with compact support contained in the open half-line), then the transfer function $$\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. For any $b>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$, the full entire-plane bound is $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}\|K_{jk}\prime\prime\|_1|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$. Its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi$$ for every real $\omega$.

(c) (Integrable branch.) If instead $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is locally absolutely continuous entrywise in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]] on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$, with $K\prime$ its almost-everywhere derivative with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $s\mapsto sK(s)$ in $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, then $\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on the open upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the same pair of dispersion relations for every real $\omega$, and is bounded on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ by $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}$ for $|z|\ge1$; for an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$ and apply the relations to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$.

(d) (Monochromatic work and passivity.) Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be a real parameter (a response normalization; the equivalence below is independent of its value). Put $E(t):=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t):=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, real parts taken componentwise and $\chi(\omega)$ acting by matrix multiplication. Then, with $T:=2\pi/\omega$ and the Euclidean dot product on $\mathbb R^d$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T E(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),\qquad e^*\chi(\omega)e:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\overline{e_j}\,\chi_{jk}(\omega)\,e_k,$$ and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$ if and only if the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega):=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$.
current_affected_interface_subjects.current_strategy:
Proof technique: direct, branch by branch; clausal tags below indicate the cited tools.

(a) For each $j$ and $t$, absolute convergence and the displayed bound follow from $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$, the triangle inequality for integrals and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral over the measurable set $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]). Linearity in $E$ is linearity of the integral. Continuity in $t$: if $t_n\to t$ then $K_{jk}(s)E_k(t_n-s)\to K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$ for every $s$ with the integrable dominating function $(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}|$, so dominated convergence gives $P(t_n)\to P(t)$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Causality: for $t\le t_0$ and every $s\ge0$ the argument $t-s$ lies in $(-\infty,t_0]$, so replacing $E$ by a history agreeing with it there changes no integrand value and hence no integral.

(b) Holomorphy is obtained from the real-parameter differentiation theorem rather than by differentiating in the complex variable directly. Writing $z=x+iy$, the integrand $K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}=K_{jk}(s)e^{ixs}e^{-ys}$ has continuous partials in $x$ and $y$; because $K_{jk}$ has compact support, on every compact set of parameters $(x,y)$ the partials are dominated by a fixed multiple of $|K_{jk}|(1+|s|)$, an integrable function, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied in the two real parameters gives the continuous partials $\partial_x\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ and $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). These satisfy $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=-\int sK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\int isK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}$, the Cauchy--Riemann equations for the pair $(\partial_x\chi_{jk},\partial_y\chi_{jk})$ with the identification $f=u+iv$; since the partials exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous, [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]] makes $\chi_{jk}$ holomorphic, and because the same argument is available at every $z\in\mathbb C$, each entry is entire ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Iterating gives $\chi_{jk}^{(k)}(z)=\int_0^\infty(is)^kK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$. For the reality identity at real $\omega$: conjugation is an isometry and a real-field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and the series defining the complex exponential converges everywhere ([[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]); conjugating the partial sums termwise and passing to the limit along the isometry gives $\overline{e^{i\omega s}}=e^{-i\omega s}$, so conjugating the defining integral of $\chi_{jk}$ and using that $K_{jk}$ is real gives $\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}\,ds=\chi_{jk}(-\omega)$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). On $[0,b]$, apply [[thm-integration-by-parts]] twice to the real and imaginary parts of the smooth exponential and real smooth kernel (first $K$, then $K\prime$). All derivatives are continuous and Riemann integrable; [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]] transfers each compact-interval identity to the Lebesgue integrals. With vanishing endpoint values because $K$ vanishes near $0$ and beyond $b$, these identities give $\chi_{jk}(z)=-z^{-2}\int_0^\infty K_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the stated upper-half-plane $|z|^{-2}$ bound; for arbitrary complex $z$, $|e^{izs}|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ on the support gives the full entire-plane bound. For the dispersion relations fix real $\omega$ and form a contour consisting of the interval $[-R,R]$ indented above $\omega$ on a clockwise semicircle of radius $\delta$, closed by the large semicircle of radius $R$ in the upper half-plane; on the indented domain the integrand $\chi_{jk}(z)/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic, so Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops gives vanishing total integral ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]]). The large arc contributes at most $\pi R\sup_{|z|=R,\operatorname{Im}z\ge0}|\chi_{jk}|/(R-|\omega|)\to0$ by the $|z|^{-2}$ bound. The small arc contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\delta\to0$, by continuity of $\chi_{jk}$ on the closed upper half-plane, which follows from dominated convergence as in (a) ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). The remaining real integral converges to its principal value: near $\omega$ subtract the constant $\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ so that the divided difference $[\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded, and at infinity use the $|z|^{-2}$ decay. Letting $\delta\to0$, $R\to\infty$ gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating real and imaginary parts yields the displayed pair because $i(a+ib)=-b+ia$.

(c) This is precisely the content of the cited integrable-causal-dispersion lemma: that item proves, under exactly these hypotheses, the holomorphy on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]), the closed-half-plane bound, the boundary regularity and the two principal-value formulas, and records the instantaneous-response subtraction ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]). The present theorem assembles the response, its transfer function and the passivity relation around that lemma; its explicit AC definition and Lebesgue FTC/integration-by-parts route apply entrywise under the inherited Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; its boundary contour uses vertical shifts before passing to the real boundary.

(d) The period-average of a product of real parts of complex exponentials is supplied by [[lem-em-period-average]], which states exactly $\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})dt=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\cdot\overline d)$; applying it with $a=e$ and $d=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ (the derivative of $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, computed with the chain rule) gives $$\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e\cdot\overline{(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e}\Bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),$$ using $e\cdot\overline{\chi(\omega)e}=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-iz)=\operatorname{Im}z$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]). Finally $e^*M(\omega)e=(e^*\chi(\omega)e-e^*\chi(\omega)^*e)/(2i)=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ because $M(\omega)$ is the Hermitian dissipative part of $\chi(\omega)$, so nonnegativity of the displayed average for every $e$ is exactly the stated quadratic-form condition. The logical independence of causality and this positivity (the design's 'no sign of dissipation follows merely from causality') is exhibited on the companion example page by a kernel satisfying (c) whose quadratic form is strictly negative.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the surface-integral conventions used by [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]].

(i) (Causality without passivity.) In this clause also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]), inherited from the exact AC supplier. Let $K(s):=-e^{-s}$ for $s\ge0$. Then $K$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ (indeed $K'=e^{-s}=-K$, $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=1$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$), so the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] applies: $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ is a bounded causal linear response on bounded continuous histories, its transfer function is $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and its boundary value $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ for every $\omega>0$. Hence the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$ is strictly negative, not positive semidefinite, and the monochromatic period-averaged work of clause (d) of that theorem is strictly negative for $d=1$, every $e\ne0$ and every $\omega>0$ (with any response normalization $\varepsilon_0>0$), although the response is causal and its entry satisfies the dispersion relations of clause (c). Nonnegative period-averaged work (passivity) is therefore an additional condition on the model, not a consequence of temporal causality.

(ii) (The flux limit needs fixed retarded time.) In the setting of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]], fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in S^2$, and let $r>\max\{2a,\;a+c(t-t_0)\}$. Then for every $y\in B_a$ one has $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$, so $t-R/c<t_0$; by hypothesis (H1) of that theorem the functions $\rho,\rho_t,\mathbf J,\mathbf J_t$ all vanish at $(y,t-R/c)$, so every integrand in the field formulas of clause (a) of that theorem vanishes and $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$, hence $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. Therefore $\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)\,d\Omega(n)=0$ for all such $r$: at fixed observation time the far-zone flux integral is identically zero beyond the light cone of the compact spacetime support, whereas clause (c) of that theorem is a limit at fixed retarded time. The retarded-time formulation cannot be replaced by a fixed-observation-time one.
current_affected_interface_subjects.current_strategy:
Proof technique: direct computation and direct substitution into the two cited theorems.

(i) The real exponential is differentiable with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]) and $\exp(-s)>0$ with $\exp(-s)=1/\exp(s)$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]), so $s\mapsto K(s)=-e^{-s}$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K'=e^{-s}=-K$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). For every $N>0$ the Newton-Leibniz formula gives $\int_0^Ne^{-s}ds=1-e^{-N}$ and integration by parts (with $u=s$, $v=-e^{-s}$) gives $\int_0^Nse^{-s}ds=1-(1+N)e^{-N}$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], [[thm-integration-by-parts]]); the continuous real integrands have the same Lebesgue integrals by [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]; [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]] proves the explicit $C^1$ kernel is absolutely continuous on each compact interval in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]; the displayed Newton-Leibniz integral representations agree with the Lebesgue FTC under this regularity. Thus it has the absolute-continuity property required by the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]], and passing to the limit with monotone convergence for the nonnegative integrands gives $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$, so $K,K',sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). Clause (a) of the theorem therefore gives the bounded causal response. For the transfer function, fix real $\omega$; the complex exponential is entire with derivative itself and the complex chain rule gives that $s\mapsto F(s)=\exp((-1+i\omega)s)/(-1+i\omega)$ is a primitive of $s\mapsto\exp((-1+i\omega)s)$ on $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]], [[def-complex-exponential]]), so the fundamental theorem for complex line integrals along the interval path $[0,N]\ni s\mapsto s$ gives $\int_{[0,N]}\exp((-1+i\omega)s)\,ds=F(N)-F(0)$ ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-for-complex-line-integrals]], [[def-complex-primitive]], [[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]], [[thm-riemann-stieltjes-and-parametric-contour-integrals-agree]]). Hence $\int_0^N(-e^{-s})e^{i\omega s}ds=-(F(N)-F(0))$, and $\left|e^{(-1+i\omega)N}\right|=e^{-N}\to0$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]); letting $N\to\infty$ with dominated convergence for the integrands dominated by $e^{-s}$ gives $\chi(\omega)=-1/(1-i\omega)$, and the same computation with $z$ in place of $\omega$ gives $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Taking real and imaginary parts ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) gives $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ and $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ because $\omega>0$. With $d=1$, $e=1$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, clause (d) of the theorem gives period-averaged work $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)<0$ and $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)<0$, so the passivity condition fails while causality holds: this witnesses the logical independence recorded in the theorem's proof discussion.

(ii) For $y\in B_a$ the reverse triangle inequality gives $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), hence $t-R/c<t_0$ and all four source functions vanish at the arguments appearing in the field integrals of clause (a) of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]]; each integrand is identically zero on $B_a$, so $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$ and therefore $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=\mu_0^{-1}n\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. The surface integral of the zero function vanishes ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), so the fixed-observation-time flux integral is $0$ for every $r>\max\{2a,a+c(t-t_0)\}$, while the limit displayed in clause (c) of that theorem is taken with $u$ fixed and $r\to\infty$ along $t=u+r/c$; the two formulations therefore differ and the retarded-time one is essential.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq\Omega$. For $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ let $s=s(x,t)$ be the unique retarded root of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and put $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $N:=n\cdot\beta$, $D:=\kappa r$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ and $d:=n\cdot\dot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) the distributions $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\,\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,$$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. (b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals
$$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad
\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds.$$
Here the second integral is componentwise. The notation $\varepsilon_0^{-1}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle$ and $\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, if used, means precisely these explicit history integrals, rather than ordinary distribution action on a compactly supported test. These pairings define distributions on $\Omega$, are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$ (for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the $C^2$ functions $$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$ off the worldline, and the zero extensions $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ on $\Gamma$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\widetilde\varphi$, and $\Upsilon$ that of $\widetilde A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function|regular distribution]]). (c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Then, off the worldline, $$E=C\left[\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r}\right],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}.$$ The fields $E,B$ are $C^1$ off the worldline. More generally, if $z\in C^k$, $k\ge3$, the retarded root is $C^k$, the potentials are $C^{k-1}$ and the fields are $C^{k-2}$ there; if $z\in C^\infty$, all these objects are smooth off the worldline. The result is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated uniformly subluminal smooth worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved.
current_affected_interface_subjects.current_strategy:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as stipulated in the statement. (a) Apply [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] to the $C^1$ curve $z$ on $\mathbb R$; $C^3$ is a special case, and its all-time graph is proper because a compact ambient set bounds the time coordinate.
(b) Fix a compact observation set $Q\subseteq\{(x,t):|x|\le M,\ t_0\le t\le t_1\}$, and tests supported in $Q$. If $g(s,y):=(z(s)+y,s+|y|/c)\in Q$, then $s\le t_1$. For $s\le0$, using $|z(s)|\le Z+v_*|s|$ with $Z:=|z(0)|$ gives
$$t_0\le s+|y|/c=s+|x-z(s)|/c\le -(1-v_*/c)|s|+(M+Z)/c.$$
Thus $s\ge-S$, where $S:=\max\{0,(M+Z-ct_0)/(c-v_*)\}$. If $[-S,t_1]$ is empty no contributing point exists. Otherwise set $H:=\max(S,|t_1|)$ and $L:=1+M+Z+v_*H$. Every contributing $y$ has $|y|\le M+|z(s)|<L$. Consequently the pulled-back support lies in the bounded closed cylinder $[-S,t_1]\times\overline B_L$, possibly approaching $y=0$; it need not be compact inside $U:=\mathbb R\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.
On that cylinder, $|\psi(g(s,y))|/(4\pi|y|)\le\|\psi\|_\infty/(4\pi|y|)$. The polar formula [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] gives $\int_{B_L}|y|^{-1}dy=\sigma(S^2)L^2/2<\infty$. Borel product identification [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] and the Euclidean/product-measure bridge [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] allow [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] for the absolute value. Then [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] identifies the double integral with the explicit iterated history integral. In particular, with $T:=\max(0,t_1+S)$ and $M_Q:=T\sigma(S^2)L^2/(8\pi)$,
$$|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|\le |q|M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty/\varepsilon_0,\qquad
|\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle|\le\mu_0|q|v_*M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty.$$
The seminorm $\psi\mapsto|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|$ restricts continuously to each fixed-support test space by these bounds, and likewise for each component of $\Upsilon$. Thus [[def-test-function-topology]] and [[def-distribution]] prove distribution continuity directly; no action of $\rho$ or $J$ on a noncompact test is assumed.
The graph $\Gamma$ is closed: convergence of $(z(s_j),s_j)$ forces $s_j\to t$ and $z(s_j)\to z(t)$. Thus $V:=\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ is open. On $U$, $g$ is $C^1$, and in coordinate order $(s,y_1,y_2,y_3)$ its determinant is $-\kappa(s,y)$, with $\kappa=1-(y/|y|)\cdot z'(s)/c\ge1-v_*/c>0$. If $g(s,y)=g(s',y')$, then $|s-s'|=||y'|-|y||/c\le|z(s')-z(s)|/c\le(v_*/c)|s-s'|$, so $s=s'$ and $y=y'$. No image point belongs to $\Gamma$: otherwise $|y|=|z(t)-z(s)|\le v_*(t-s)=v_*|y|/c$, contradicting $y\ne0$. Conversely every point of $V$ has the unique retarded root supplied by [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]], giving inverse $(x,t)\mapsto(s(x,t),x-z(s(x,t)))$. Its $C^1$ regularity follows from that supplier's $C^3$ branch on the open domain $x\ne z(t)$, using this consumer's $C^3$ hypothesis. No exclusion of the entire spatial trajectory is imposed. Therefore $g:U\to V$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.
For any compact $Q\subseteq\Omega$, the nonnegative Borel substitution lemma [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]] applied to $1_Q/(\kappa r)$ on $V$ yields
$$\int_V\frac{1_Q}{\kappa r}\,dx\,dt=\int_U\frac{1_Q(g(s,y))}{|y|}\,ds\,dy<\infty.$$
The same bound holds for $|\beta|/(c\kappa r)$ since $|\beta|\le v_*/c$. Extend the potentials by zero on the closed graph. These extensions are Borel and locally integrable on all of $\Omega$. Applying the same Borel substitution first to the absolute value of $\psi/(\kappa r)$ establishes its $L^1$ integrability on $V$, and [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]] then gives the scalar pairing formula in the statement. Apply it componentwise to $z'(s)$-weighted data for the vector formula. Its prefactor is
$$\frac{\mu_0qz'(s)}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0qc\beta}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0c\varepsilon_0 C\beta}{\kappa r}=\frac{C\beta}{c\kappa r},$$
since $\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0=1$. The regular-distribution identities mean the zero extensions, as in [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]; tests may be nonzero on $\Gamma$. The retarded root is $C^3$ on $V$, and $r,n$ are $C^3$ while $\beta,\kappa,D$ are $C^2$ with $D>0$, so the potentials are $C^2$. The same composition argument gives the matching $C^k$ and $C^\infty$ branches.
(c) Derivatives of the retarded data: from $t-s=r/c$ and R1, $\nabla s=-n/(c\kappa)$, $s_t=1/\kappa$, hence $\nabla r=n/\kappa$ and $r_t=-cN/\kappa$ (chain rule, [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); $R=x-z(s)$ gives $\partial_iR=e_i+\beta\,n_i/\kappa$ and $\beta=z'(s)/c$ gives $\partial_i\beta=-\dot\beta\,n_i/(c\kappa)$, while $\beta_t=\dot\beta/\kappa$ (componentwise chain rule and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). Since $D=r-R\cdot\beta$, the product rules for the Euclidean pairing give $D_t=r_t-R_t\cdot\beta-R\cdot\beta_t=(c(|\beta|^2-N)-rd)/\kappa$ and $\partial_iD=\partial_ir-(\partial_iR)\cdot\beta-R\cdot\partial_i\beta$, hence $\nabla D=((1-|\beta|^2+rd/c)/\kappa)\,n-\beta$; the required product rules are the coordinatewise one-variable product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then $\varphi=C/D$ gives $\nabla\varphi=-C\nabla D/D^2$, $\varphi_t=-CD_t/D^2$, and $A=\beta\varphi/c$ gives $A_t=(\beta_t\varphi+\beta\varphi_t)/c=\dot\beta C/(c\kappa D)-\beta CD_t/(cD^2)$, so $$E=-\nabla\varphi-A_t=\frac{C}{D^2}\Bigl(\nabla D+\frac{\beta D_t}{c}\Bigr)-\frac{C\dot\beta}{c\kappa D}.$$ The bracket equals $\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)+(rd/c)(n-\beta)}{\kappa}$ (substituting the two displayed identities and $\kappa=1-N$), and writing the second term over the common denominator $\kappa^3r^2$ replaces its numerator by $-r\kappa\dot\beta/c$, giving $E=\frac{C}{\kappa^3r^2}\bigl[(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)+\frac{r}{c}\bigl(d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta\bigr)\bigr]$; the coordinate triple-product identity $n\times((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta)=d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta$ (expand both sides with [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]) yields the displayed $E$. For the magnetic field, $\operatorname{curl}(\beta\varphi/c)=\nabla(\varphi/c)\times\beta+(\varphi/c)\operatorname{curl}\beta$ ([[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]), and $\operatorname{curl}\beta=\nabla s\times\dot\beta$ by the coordinate formula applied to $\beta=z'(s(x,t))/c$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); substituting $\nabla\varphi=-C\nabla D/D^2$ and $\nabla s=-n/(c\kappa)$ gives $$B=-C\left[\frac{1-|\beta|^2+rd/c}{c\kappa D^2}\,n\times\beta+\frac{n\times\dot\beta}{c^2\kappa D}\right].$$ Crossing the displayed $E$ with $n/c$ gives this same expression by $n\times(n-\beta)=-n\times\beta$ and $D=\kappa r$, proving $B=n\times E/c$. Both displayed fields are $C^1$ off the worldline, and no derivative of $z$ beyond the third order and no bound on $\Gamma$ at infinity is used; the caveats in the statement are exactly those of the research branch argument.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. (i) Static specialization. Take $z\equiv0$ (so $v_*=0$), $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, in the setting of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]. Then for $x\ne0$ the root is $s=t-|x|/c$, $r=|x|$, $n=x/|x|$, $\beta=0$, $\kappa=1$, $\dot\beta=0$, so the potentials and fields are $\varphi=C/|x|$, $A=0$, $E=C\,x/|x|^3$, $B=0$. Thus the retarded formulas reduce exactly to the Coulomb field with the convention $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and the kernel's explicit retarded-history integral reproduces the time-independent Poisson kernel $1/(4\pi|x-y|)$: for a static spatial source $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, define the all-time retarded extension by
$$u(x,t):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy.$$
Indeed the retarded time is $t-|x-y|/c$ and evaluating the static source there leaves $h(y)$ unchanged. This finite integral is the extension of the compact spacetime-source formula by source-time cutoffs on each compact observation region; a time-independent nonzero source is not itself compactly supported in spacetime. (ii) Explicit Lorenz-gauge transformation. On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ take $\varphi\equiv0$ and $A(x,t)=(x_1,0,0)$. Then $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A=1$ and $E=-\partial_tA=0$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A=0$. The quadratic function $\chi(x,t):=-|x|^2/6$ satisfies $W\chi=G$: indeed $\partial_t^2\chi=0$ and $\Delta\chi=-1$, so $W\chi=c^{-2}\cdot0-(-1)=1=G$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Its gauge transform is $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(0,\ ((2/3)x_1,-x_2/3,-x_3/3))$, which satisfies $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=\frac23-\frac13-\frac13=0$ and has the same fields: $E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=0=E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=0=B(\varphi,A)$. This checks clauses (b) and (c) of [[lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability]] in an instance where $G$ is a nonzero constant and where the gauge function does not have the zero Cauchy data used in the existence construction of that lemma; by its clause (d), the difference of this $\chi$ and the zero-data solution of $W\chi=G$ solves the homogeneous wave equation, which is why both may be used. (iii) Sharpness of the kernel support at the apex. For a nonnegative $\psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ with $\psi(0,0)>0$ one has $\langle K,\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\psi(y,|y|/c)|y|^{-1}dy>0$, so $(0,0)\in\operatorname{supp}K$ and the apex is not an artefact of the definition; the same computation with a bump near $(y_0,|y_0|/c)$, $y_0\ne0$, shows that every point of the cone is in the support. These are mathematical checks of the pair's conventions and hypotheses; no measurement, physical field identification, or empirical claim is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the change-of-variables corollaries inside the proof of the retarded-convolution identity cited in clause (b) ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, let $v_*<c$, let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$.

(a) [Root and emission-time Jacobian] For every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ (equivalently $x\ne z(t)$) there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. The map $s:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) one has $$\partial_ts(x,t)=\kappa^{-1},\qquad \nabla_xs(x,t)=-\frac{n}{c\,\kappa},\qquad \kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c],$$ so $\kappa\ge 1-v_*/c>0$ uniformly on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. Moreover, for the fixed $x$ and near the root, the function $s'\mapsto s'+|x-z(s')|/c$ is differentiable at $s'=s$ with derivative $\kappa(x,t)$: this emission-time Jacobian $1-n\cdot\beta$ is the denominator produced by the delta substitution of clause (b).

(b) [Delta substitution and Liénard-Wiechert potentials] Let $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the point-source distributions of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] attached to $q$ and the worldline $z$, let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]], and for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$ and define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=(q/\varepsilon_0)\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds$, $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds$, componentwise in the second case. These are the history-integral interpretation supplied by clause(b) of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]], not ordinary distribution action on a noncompact test. Then these pairings are finite for every $\psi$ and their exact retarded-convolution values are $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt$$ (the second identity componentwise); equivalently, $\Phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are the regular distributions of the locally integrable zero extensions to $\Gamma$ of the $C^2$ functions $\varphi:=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A:=\beta\varphi/c$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. The weight $(\kappa r)^{-1}$ with $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ is the exact form of the substitution with denominator $1-n\cdot\beta$ (the rigorous statement is the displayed pairing identity; composition of $\delta$ with a function is not part of the distribution calculus used here).

(c) [Fields and the velocity/acceleration split] With $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]), and writing $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ at the root, $$E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{vel}}=\frac{C(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2},\qquad E_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r},\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}$$ at every event of $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). Both $E$ and $B$ are $C^1$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, and the velocity field obeys the bound $$|E_{\mathrm{vel}}(x,t)|\le |C|\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r(x,t)^{-2}$$ at every event.

(d) [Uniform far-zone remainder] For every $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and every $n\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|n|=1$, put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$ and $t_r:=s_0+r/c$ for $r>0$, and set $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $\dot\beta_0:=z''(s_0)/c$, $\kappa_0:=1-n\cdot\beta_0$. Then $(x_r,t_r)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$ for every $r>0$, and $$E(x_r,t_r)=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0\bigr)}{c\,\kappa_0^3\,r}+\rho_E(s_0,n,r),\qquad B(x_r,t_r)=\frac{n\times E(x_r,t_r)}{c},$$ where the remainder is bounded uniformly in the direction, $$|\rho_E(s_0,n,r)|\le |C|\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r^{-2}\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2\text{ and every }r>0.$$ Equivalently, $rE(x_r,t_r)\to C\,n\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)/(c\,\kappa_0^3)$ as $r\to\infty$, uniformly over $n\in S^2$ at the explicit rate $O(r^{-1})$ given by the same bound multiplied by $r$. The uniformity is in the direction $n$ at a fixed emission event $s_0$; no uniformity in $s_0$ is asserted ($z''$ is not assumed bounded), and no finite-energy, decay or radiation-flux conclusion is drawn.

This is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated $C^3$ uniformly subluminal worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved, and the uniform speed bound and the exclusion of $\Gamma$ are essential hypotheses (see the companion example page).

(i) [Plane-wave solutions with infinite spatial $L^2$ norm] Let $c>0$ and $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as in [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function $u:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $u(x,t):=f(x_1-ct)$, is of class $C^\infty$ and satisfies $Wu=0$ identically. If $f\ne0$, then for every $t$ the level set $\{x:u(x,t)\ne0\}=(ct+U)\times\mathbb R^2$, where $U:=\{s\in\mathbb R:f(s)\ne0\}$ is nonempty and open, is unbounded, and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(x,t)|^2\,dx=+\infty$. Consequently the smooth-data existence and smoothness clause (a) of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] carries no global finite-energy or decay conclusion: compact support of the data is a genuine hypothesis of its clause (d), not a consequence of smoothness.

(ii) [Failure of root existence without the uniform speed bound] Let $c>0$, $a>0$ and $z(s):=(\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2},0,0)$. Then $z$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with $|z'(s)|=\dfrac{c^2|s|}{\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2}}<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$, while $\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|z'(s)|=c$; so there is no $v_*<c$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$: the worldline is subluminal at every finite time but has no uniform subluminal bound. For the observation $(x,t)=(0,0)$ there is no root $s<t$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$: the equation would read $-s=\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2}/c$ with $s<0$, and squaring gives $s^2=s^2+a^2/c^2$, i.e. $a=0$, a contradiction. Thus the existence clause of [[thm-em-retarded-root-and-fields]] genuinely needs its hypothesis $|z'|\le v_*<c$; the substitution denominator degenerates along this curve in the same limit.

(iii) [The event must lie off the worldline] Let $z$ be of class $C^1$ with $|z'|\le v_*<c$, and let $x=z(t)$ for some $t\in\mathbb R$. Then $s=t$ solves $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$ trivially, and the strict decrease of $s\mapsto t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ shows that no root $s<t$ exists; hence the exclusion of the worldline $\Gamma$ in clause (a) of [[thm-em-retarded-root-and-fields]] is a genuine hypothesis.

These are explicit mathematical checks of hypotheses and conventions of the wave and retarded-root results; no measurement, physical field identification or empirical claim is made.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Let U be a nonempty open subset of A which, with the manifold topology of lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas, is path-connected and simply connected (def-simply-connected), and let alpha be a C^1 one-form on U with d alpha = 0 (def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms). Consequently, for any two piecewise C^1 paths gamma_0, gamma_1 in U with the same endpoints the integrals of alpha along them are equal, and the integral of alpha along every piecewise C^1 loop in U vanishes. Here for a C^1 one-form, closedness means in an inertial chart alpha=sum_i a_i dx^i with partial_i a_j=partial_j a_i; the exterior derivative is understood by this coefficient formula. current_affected_interface_subjects.current_strategy:

(1) Local C^1 primitive, supplied in full rather than invoking the smooth-only imported Poincare theorem. On any convex ball B contained in U, fix b in B and set phi(x)=integral_0^1 sum_i a_i(b+t(x-b))(x_i-b_i) dt. For x in B and sufficiently small h, the radial segments for x+h e_j lie in a compact subset of B. The parameter derivative of the integrand is continuous on that compact set. The one-variable FTC expresses its difference quotient as the average of that derivative along x+u h e_j; uniform continuity makes these averages converge uniformly in t. Hence taking the integral of the quotient gives partial_j phi(x)=integral_0^1 [a_j(b+t(x-b))+t sum_i (x_i-b_i) partial_j a_i(b+t(x-b))]dt. Closedness and the chain rule identify the integrand with d/dt[t a_j(b+t(x-b))], so FTC gives partial_j phi=a_j. These partial derivatives are continuous, hence phi is C^1; since all a_j are C^1, phi is C^2. Chain rule and FTC on each path piece give integral_gamma alpha=phi(gamma(1))-phi(gamma(0)) for every piecewise-C^1 path contained in B. This is the C^1 radial proof of Lebl Thm 9.3.6, written explicitly here.
(2) Compact small-cell construction. Given a continuous based null-homotopy H:[0,1]^2 -> U of a piecewise-C^1 loop gamma at p, compactness of K=H([0,1]^2) gives finitely many balls B(b_l,r_l) contained in U whose concentric half-radius balls cover K. To obtain this finite family, cover K by all pairs of such balls centered at points of K; use compactness, then finitely many witnesses. Set r=min_l r_l>0. Uniform continuity of H gives delta>0 such that domain distances less than delta imply image distances less than r/2. Choose a finite rectangular mesh with cell diameter less than delta. For each cell, its lower-left image vertex belongs to a half-radius ball; the entire cell image is therefore contained in the corresponding full-radius ball. Only finitely many ball assignments are made. Refine the bottom mesh by the finitely many breakpoints of gamma if desired; this preserves the small-cell property.
(3) Replace each oriented mesh edge by the affine straight segment between its two image vertices. Each cell's four segments lie in its assigned convex ball, so its boundary integral is zero by (1). Every shared edge is exactly the same segment traversed oppositely by the adjacent cell; therefore finite summation cancels all interior edges. The top and vertical boundary segments are constant, since the homotopy is based. Each bottom loop arc and its replacement chord lie in the ball assigned to the corresponding bottom cell, so (1) makes their integrals equal. Thus integral_gamma alpha=0. No differentiability of H or smoothing theorem is used. The argument needs only continuous based null-homotopies, which the simply-connected definition supplies at every basepoint.
(4) For any two piecewise-C^1 paths from p to q, concatenate the first with the reversed second. It is a loop with zero integral by (3); finite concatenation and reversal give equal integrals. The resulting polygonal path stays in U and has the same endpoints.
(5) Fix p0 in the nonempty U. For each x let F(x) be the unique real value of the integral over a piecewise-C^1 path from p0 to x; existence follows from (4), and path independence makes the value unique. (a) Inertial worldline. A curve x: I -> A is inertial (also called uniform or straight) when there are a parameter value s_0 in I, an event p in A and a vector d in V, with d future timelike, such that x(s) = p + (s - s_0) d for every s in I. If two inertial worldlines have the same image and the same direction of traversal, then each is an increasing affine reparametrization of the other: with x(s) = p + (s - s_0) d and y(t) = p' + (t - t_0) d' one has d' = alpha d with alpha > 0 and p' = p + mu d, hence y(t) = x(s_0 + mu + alpha(t - t_0)). A curve x: [a,b] -> A is piecewise inertial when there are a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b, events p_1,...,p_m in A and future timelike vectors d_1,...,d_m in V such that x(s) = p_i + (s - s_{i-1}) d_i for every s in [s_{i-1}, s_i] and every i = 1,...,m, and consecutive pieces agree at the partition points, that is p_{i+1} = p_i + (s_i - s_{i-1}) d_i = x(s_i) for i = 1,...,m-1. The definition asserts the existence of no further worldlines and attaches no clock reading to the curves; readings are the subject of the model's postulates.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Work in the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (A,V,eta,C^+) (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) with its inertial atlas (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas) and the canonical identification T_pA = V (lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v). The following objects are defined and are, in general, different objects. (a) Chart and inertial chart. A chart of the model is a diffeomorphism u: U -> u(U) from a nonempty open subset U of A onto an open subset of R^4 (def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds, def-smooth-manifold), written with components (u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3). An inertial chart (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart) is the global chart x(p) = E^{-1}(p-o) of an inertial frame (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3). A general chart need not be inertial: if x is an inertial chart and N: x(U) -> R^4 is a diffeomorphism onto its image which is not the restriction of an affine map, then u := N o x is a chart that is not inertial, because if u were the inertial chart of a frame then x o u^{-1} = N^{-1} would be affine by lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz and hence N = (N^{-1})^{-1} would be affine as the inverse of an affine bijection, a contradiction; the map N(y) = (y^0, y^1 + (y^0)^2, y^2, y^3) on R^4 is an explicit example. (b) Tetrad at an event and tetrad field. A tetrad at p in A is an ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) of V with eta(e_a,e_b) = diag(-1,1,1,1)_{ab} and e_0 future (e_0 in C^+); this is an inertial frame's basis without an origin and without the orientation condition. A tetrad field on a nonempty open subset Omega of A is a tuple (E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3) of smooth vector fields on Omega (def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space, type (1,0)) whose values at every p form a tetrad at p; it is observer-adapted when E_0 = U/c for a prescribed future timelike worldline or congruence. (c) Observer congruence. An observer congruence on a nonempty open subset Omega of A is a smooth vector field n: Omega -> V with eta(n,n) = -1 and n(p) in C^+ for all p; its observers are its maximal integral curves (def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field, thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point), each of which is a future timelike worldline (def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline); n is nowhere zero because it is unit. Completeness of the integral curves, a global product structure of Omega and global synchronization are not asserted. (d) Adapted chart. For a congruence n on Omega, an n-adapted chart is a chart (u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3): U -> R^4 with U a nonempty open subset of Omega whose spatial coordinates u^1,u^2,u^3 are constant along every integral curve of n contained in U; no global adapted chart is asserted, and u^0 is not required to be affine. (e) Distinctions. A chart need not be inertial (a); a chart need not be n-adapted for any congruence; a tetrad field is not in general the coordinate frame of a chart: if (E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3) is the coordinate frame of a chart (v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3), i.e. E_a = partial/partial v^a, then [E_a,E_b] = 0 for all a,b (def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields, prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket), so a tetrad field whose members do not commute pairwise is not a coordinate frame; no converse is claimed here. A congruence need not be a coordinate flow, and its pointwise rest spaces need not assemble into hypersurfaces; that integrability question is decided below on this page. In an inertial chart the coordinate frame is simultaneously an inertial frame's basis, a constant tetrad field and the congruence of stationary observers, but the four notions are distinct in general.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Let c>0 be the conversion constant of def-sr-proper-time and let x:[a,b]->A, a<b, be a piecewise C^1 future timelike worldline in the weak sense of def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline: x is C^1 on each open piece of a finite partition a=s_0<...<s_m=b, its interior tangents and finite one-sided difference-quotient endpoint tangents are future timelike, and continuous extension of the derivative is not assumed. (i) On each open piece let g_i(t)=sqrt(-eta(x'(t),x'(t)))>0. Define its two-ended improper Riemann integral by the convention of lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability. That lemma proves each value finite and nonnegative; it is positive since g_i is positive and continuous on a compact interior subinterval. (ii) Define total proper time by Delta tau_[a,b](x)=c^{-1} sum_i integral_(s_(i-1),s_i) g_i. The finite sum is independent of the partition, by subdivision additivity and a common refinement. It is independent of the inertial chart because eta and the tangent are chart independent; constant Lorentz changes preserve the density already on each proper truncation. (iii) Define the based proper-time function tau_x(s)=Delta tau_[s0,s](x) for s>=s0, and tau_x(s)=-Delta tau_[s,s0](x) for s<s0, with tau_x(s0)=0, using restrictions and oriented limits. It is strictly increasing, and changing s0 changes only an additive constant. (iv) Corner hypothesis (H) is the special case in which each open-piece derivative has finite limits at both ends and thus extends continuously to the closed piece. Those limits equal the one-sided quotient derivatives. Under (H), each g_i extends continuously and positively to the closed piece, its improper integral equals its ordinary Riemann integral there, and the same finite-sum formula applies. In particular if x is globally C^1 on [a,b], Delta tau(x)=tau(b)-tau(a) of def-sr-proper-time. (v) Delta tau(x)>0. If on piece i the tangent is a constant future timelike vector d_i, the contribution is c^{-1}(s_i-s_(i-1))sqrt(-eta(d_i,d_i)); this gives the finite sum of straight-segment proper times. (vi) Additivity over concatenation: for a<b<d, restrictions of a weak piecewise worldline x on [a,d] satisfy Delta tau_[a,d](x)=Delta tau_[a,b](x)+Delta tau_[b,d](x). Insert b in the partition and use (ii). The definition supplies metric time only; identification with an ideal clock reading is the separate physical clock postulate. No global C^1 inverse, tangent at a kink, or four-acceleration at a kink is asserted.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and use the reachability objects J^+, I^+ of def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space. Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame with chart x (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart) and let |v_s| := sqrt((v^1)^2 + (v^2)^2 + (v^3)^2) be the Euclidean norm of the spatial part v_s := v^1 e_1 + v^2 e_2 + v^3 e_3 of a vector v = v^0 e_0 + v_s (def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame). Then: (a) Cone description. C^+ = {v : v^0 > |v_s|}, Cbar^+ = {v : v^0 >= |v_s|}, C^- = {v : -v^0 > |v_s|} and Cbar^- = {v : -v^0 >= |v_s|}; moreover every v in Cbar^+ with v not 0 satisfies -eta(v,e_0) = v^0 > 0 and |v_s| <= v^0, and v is future null exactly when |v_s| = v^0 > 0. (b) Finite sums. If v_1,...,v_k are in Cbar^+ then v_1 + ... + v_k is in Cbar^+; if, in addition, at least one v_i is in C^+, then the sum is in C^+; and if v + w = 0 with v,w in Cbar^+, then v = w = 0. (c) Coordinate criterion. For events p,q in A with D^a := x^a(q) - x^a(p) and spatial part D_s := (D^1,D^2,D^3): q is in J^+(p) if and only if D^0 >= |D_s|; q is in I^+(p) if and only if D^0 > |D_s|; q is in J^+(p) with q not p if and only if D^0 >= |D_s| and D^0 > 0; and for q in J^+(p) with q not p one has 0 < D^0 and |D_s| <= D^0. The criteria are stated for the chart of any inertial frame, because every inertial basis is eta-orthonormal with future first vector. (d) Scope. The lemma is a statement about the affine model and the fixed time orientation; it attaches no physical meaning to <=, J^+ or I^+ and uses no choice principle.
current_affected_interface_subjects.current_strategy: All three clauses are coordinate algebra in one inertial basis, plus the triangle inequality. (a) In the eta-orthonormal basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) one has eta(v,v) = -(v^0)^2 + |v_s|^2 for every v (lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components), so the timelike set is T_+ union T_- with T_+ = {v : v^0 > |v_s|} and T_- = {v : v^0 < -|v_s|}, and these are the two connected components of the timelike set. Because e_0 is in C^+ and lies in T_+, the component C^+ equals T_+; the same lemma gives cl(T_+) = {v : v^0 >= |v_s|}, whence Cbar^+ = cl(C^+) = {v^0 >= |v_s|}, and the past statements follow by applying this to -v with C^- = -C^+. Since |v_s| <= v^0 = -eta(v,e_0) for v in Cbar^+, and |v_s| = v^0 is the defining equation of the nonzero null vectors of cl(T_+) with positive time component, the equality statement follows. (b) For v,w in Cbar^+ the displayed description gives (v+w)^0 = v^0 + w^0 >= |v_s| + |w_s| >= |v_s + w_s| by the triangle inequality for the Euclidean norm on span(e_1,e_2,e_3) (cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm, def-euclidean-inner-product), so v + w is in Cbar^+; if v is timelike then v^0 > |v_s| makes the first inequality strict and gives v + w in C^+. Induction on k applies the two steps successively (finite sums are defined by induction, so no choice is used). If v + w = 0 with v,w in Cbar^+, then v = -w lies in Cbar^+ intersect Cbar^- = {0} by def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. (c) q in J^+(p) means q - p in Cbar^+, and the coordinates of q - p are D by affine linearity of the chart x = E^{-1}(p - o); so (a) gives the three criteria, and D = 0 is equivalent to q = p. No choice principle is used; the only analytic input is the triangle inequality for a finite-dimensional Euclidean norm.

current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Let c > 0 and let x: I -> A be a C^1 future timelike worldline with proper-time function tau, tau(s) = c^{-1} integral_{s_0}^{s} sqrt(-eta(x'(u),x'(u))) du (def-sr-proper-time). current_affected_interface_subjects.current_statement: Adopt as a physical assumption of this framework the following restriction on signal transmission, called the causal signal restriction of the model. (i) Causal restriction. Let p and q be the emission and reception events of an idealized transmission that carries a signal, where a signal is understood as information, or a physical marker by which a prepared operation at the emission event is correlated with an observation at the reception event, within the model. Then the model admits such a transmission only if q lies in the causal future J^+(p) of p (def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space), that is, only if the displacement q - p is zero or future causal; equivalently, no signal connects an event with an event outside its closed future light cone. (ii) Ideal light. The ideal vacuum light signals of post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light are the null boundary case of the restriction: their displacement between emission and reception is future null, so in the chart of every inertial frame with x^0 = c t (def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions) they attain |x_s(q) - x_s(p)| = x^0(q) - x^0(p). (iii) Status. This is an adopted assumption about the idealized model; it is not a theorem of the affine geometry, it is not derived here from the other postulates or from any experiment, and it is not an empirical claim about nature. In particular the framework does not assert that no physical process whatsoever exceeds c, and the question whether any specified physical process is a signal of this model, and with what reliability and reach, is left to a separate experimental interface. (iv) Explicit non-restriction. The assumption does not forbid kinematic patterns in which spacelike-separated events are produced by independent prearranged mechanisms without any signal or energy transfer between them (for example a prearranged row of devices triggered in a fixed sequence), and it imposes no bound on correlations between spacelike-separated events. (v) Scope. The assumption concerns idealized point-like transmission events in the flat classical model and carries no statistical, apparatus, source or detector content; no choice principle is used.
